'''''Rabelera holostea''''', known as '''greater stitchwort''', '''greater starwort''',{{r|vascan}} and '''addersmeat''',{{r|usda}} is a perennial herbaceous [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. It was formerly placed in the genus ''[[Stellaria]]'', as '''''Stellaria holostea''''', but was transferred to the genus '''''Rabelera''''' in 2019 based on phylogenetic analyses.{{r|sharples2019}}{{r|ipni}}{{r|weakley2020}}{{r|acta}} It is the only species in the genus '''''Rabelera'''''. Greater stitchwort is native to [[Western Europe|Western]] and [[Central Europe]], including the [[British Isles]].

Greater stichwort can be found in woodlands, edges, and open fields{{r|twt}} and is sometimes grown in gardens.{{r|fowler2014}}

==Description==
Greater stitchwort can grow up to {{cvt|60|cm}} in height, with roughly 4-angled stems. The long, narrow ([[Glossary of botanical terms#lanceolate|lanceolate]]) leaves are greyish green, hairless, sessile, opposite, and [[decussation|decussate]] (the successive pairs borne at right angles to each other).{{r|stace2010}}{{rp|460}}{{r|blamey2003}}{{rp|90}}{{r|sterry1997}}

The flowers are white, {{cvt|2–3|cm}} across, with five petals split to about halfway the length of the petal. The sepals are much shorter than the petals.{{r|sterry1997}}{{r|waller1981}}

==Taxonomy==
===Etymology===
The specific epithet holostea comes from the [[Greek language|Greek]] ''holosteon'', meaning 'entire bone'; a reference to the brittleness of the weak stems of this plant.<ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/22870993 Pliny the Elder. Natural History. Book 27. Chapter 65]</ref>{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

===Common names===
The common name stitchwort is a reference to a herbal remedy in which this plant is used allegedly to cure [[side stitch]], which afflicts many people when they try to run without stretching first.{{r|firstnature}} Other common names for ''Rabelera holostea'' include: daddy's-shirt-buttons, poor-man's buttonhole, brassy buttons, wedding cakes, star-of-Bethlehem, and snapdragon.{{r|fowler2014}}{{r|twt}} Many of these names are in reference to the stems, which easily break.{{r|fowler2014}}
